latin.329:
§. III.
Ceterum propositiones S. Coenae modò dictas definitivas, & sigillatim hanc (de qua communiter disputari solet) Hoc est corpus meum, non propriam, sed impropriam esse, probant Reformati argumentis ad duo genera revocandis, quorum prius GENERICAM, posterius SPECIFICAM propositionis, materialiter acceptae, naturam concernit.
latin.330: GENERICA propositionis hujus natura (1) quà genus remotius, ostendit, Disparatum, in ea, de disparato praedicari, sive subjectum, τὸ hoc, solum panem, sive cum pane aliud praetereà, ipsum scil. Christi corpus, designet, dummodo exclusa explosaque maneat Carlstadiana Identica: Hoc Corpus est corpus meum, uti novitate & fictione, ita δισερημηνείᾳ & violentâ ab antecedentibus suis discerptione, utrique Protestantium parti merito suo exosa. Quatenus enim corpus Christi de pane, junctum licet sibi corpus Christi habente, praedicatur, praedicatur utique disparatum de disparato: At disparatorum natura, de se invicem praedicatorum, eò quòd disparata sunt, praedicationem impropriam infert, propriam respuit; sin minus, omnis praedicatio impropria è medio tollitur: Quaenam enim de se impropriè praedicabuntur, si non disparata? Certè, quicquam de seipso non potest impropriè dici: nec ulla potest dari metonymia, aut metaphora, nisi in Disparatis. Argumentum hoc si quisquam alius, acutissimè adstruxit deduxitque Doctissimus Gomarus, Operum Theol. Tom. 3. Disp. 35 a thesi 14. ad 20. inclusivè, in haec tandem Bellarmini verba definens: Non hic opus habemus Aristotele, cùm sensus communis sufficiat. Nam si liceat disparata de disparatis propriè affirmare, licebit eodem jure affirmare de nihilo aliquid, de aliquo nihil, de luce tenebras, de tenebris lucem, de Christo Belial, de Beliale Christum: neque fides nostra nos obligat ut defendamus quae contradictionem implicant pag. 139.
latin.331: Non juvat hôc loco personales objecisse praedicationes, utpote de quibus rectissimè praeceptor olim noster B. Johannes Vorstius, observat, in iis, non rem abstractam de abstracta, seu, quod idem est, disparatam naturam abstractam, de natura itidem disparata abstracta, sed concretum de concreto praedicare, cùm in sacramentali nostra, abstractum de abstracto, corpus de pane, eòque disparatum de disparato, praedicetur.
latin.332: Si instes cum Johanne Museo disp. peculiari de S. Coena, Vorstio oppositâ §. 99: In Sacramentali propositione etiam suo modo praedicari Concretum de Concreto, ita ut non dicatur: natura hujus panis est natura corporis Christi, sed tantùm, hic panis, scil. Eucharisticus, panis benedictus, non panis communis, sed Eucharistia, ex duabus rebus, terrena & caelesti, constans, est corpus Christi, citante Bajero Disp. de impanatione §.30., praeterquam quod (1) panem partim naturam abstractam relinquit esse, quatenus nempe Eucharisticus seu benedictus tantùm, nec communis ampliùs, per hoc, abstractam suam naturam nequaquam deserit, vel in concretam concedit: Neque enim panis (natura abstracta) per id, quòd ei benedictum & per benedictionem à communi usu separatus est, naturam abstractam cum concreta commutât, omni alioquin re abstractâ, & per benedictionem peculiarem à communi usu separata, per hoc ipsum in concretam convertenda; partim Eucharisticum panem, cum Eucharistia, confundit, de quorum posteriori rectè quidem dicas, ex duabus rebus, terrena & caelesti, constare, non item de priori, nisi ex sumta, nec adhuc dum probata, hypothesi, etiam (2) remanet adhuc, abstractam nihilominus naturam corporis Christi, seu abstractum corpus Christi, de concreto, seu de composito ex corpore & pane, praedicari, eòque personalibus propositionibus, (in quibus concretum, non verò abstractum, de Concreto praedicatur) praedicationem hanc sacramentalem dissimilem esse. Quando verò abstractum de Concreto directè praedicatur, uti adhucdum disparatum de disparato praedicatur, ita praedicatio non potest non esse impropria: praedicatur enim sic pars de toto, hacque ratione praedicatio conficitur synechdochica, per consequens, tropica seu impropria.
latin.333: (II) GENERICA quà genus propius, exhibet propositionem sacramentalem, in qua signatum de signo praedicatur. Etsi verò sic praedicatio propria esse possit, quando nim. Signum cum signato materialiter idem est, tamen non potest non esse impropria, quandocunque signum & signatum materialiter differunt, sive signum nude significans, sive praetereà signati exhibitivum, habeatur: Utroque enim modo praedicatio evadit vel metonymica, vel synechdochica, eòque impropria. Priori quidem, per metonymiam signi pro signato; posteriori verò, vel per metonymiam continentis pro contento, vel per synechdochen partis pro toto. Confirmatur, sacramentalem propositionem ὁριστικὴν, suâ naturâ impropriam esse, Inductione etiam singularum Sacramentalium tam Veteris, quàm N. Testamenti, in ipsa quoque S. Coenae institutione, occurrentis.
latin.334: Quando enim (a) in Institutione Circumcisionis, Deus ita Abrahamum alloquitur: Hoc est foedus meum inter me & inter vos & semen tuum post te, quod servabis, ut circumcidatur vobis omnis mas Gen. 17, 10. foedus Dei de circumcisione non nisi impropriè praedicatur: Neque enim Circumcisio propriè foedus est, sed signum foederis, Deô ipsômet interprete versu proximè sequente 11. Debetis autem praeputium carnis praescindere, hocque ipsum foederis signum futurum est inter me & vos. Quando (b) in Institutione Paschatos, totum populum, Moses, nomine Dei, ita, informat: Agnus à vobis, in star festinantium, comedendus, est pascha Domini, Exod. 12, 11. item: Accipite agnum quilibet paterfamilias pro familia sua & mactate pascha, versu 21. Item: si quis ex vobis, agno mactato vescentibus, quaesiverit: quid rei seu officii hic peragitis? Respondebitis: est Pascha sacrificium Domini filios Israelis praetereuntis in Egypto, vers. 27. in propositionibus hisce cunctis, pascha, seu transitus, tam de agno, quàm de mactatione & comesione agni, nonnisi impropriè enunciatur, substantiâ agni nequaquam in actionem transeuntem, per praedicationem aliquam propriam, convertendâ, & quidem per ejusdem speciei tropum, per quem in N. T. ipse Christus pascha nostrum dicitur 1. Cor. 5. vers. 7. nec non petra, Israelitas in deserto secuta: Solet enim res quae significat, ejus rei nomine, quam significat, nuncupari, sicut scriptum est, septem spicae septem anni sunt & multa hujusmodi. Hinc est quod dictum est petra erat Christus: non enim dixit: petra significat Christum, sed tanquam hoc esset! Utique per substantiam hoc non erat, sed per significationem, sunt verba Augustini, quaest. supra Levit. 57.

pass_a.329: §. III. For the rest, that the definitive propositions of the Sacred Supper just named — and especially this one commonly disputed, This is my body — are not proper but improper, the Reformed prove by arguments to be reduced to two genera, of which the prior concerns the GENERIC, the posterior the SPECIFIC nature of the proposition taken materially.
pass_a.330: The GENERIC nature of this proposition (1) as remoter genus shows that a Disparate is predicated in it of a disparate — whether the subject τὸ hoc designates bread alone, or besides bread something else, namely Christ’s body itself — provided the Carlstadt Identica This Body is my body remain excluded and exploded, hateful to both Protestant parties by its novelty and fiction and by δισερημηνεία and violent tearing from its antecedents. For insofar as Christ’s body is predicated of bread, even if that bread has Christ’s body joined to itself, a disparate is certainly predicated of a disparate: But the nature of disparates predicated of each other, because they are disparates, brings in improper predication and rejects the proper; otherwise every improper predication is removed from the midst: For what things will be improperly predicated of each other, if not disparates? Certainly nothing can be said improperly of itself: nor can any metonymy or metaphor be given except in Disparates. This argument, if anyone else, the most learned Gomarus most acutely built and deduced, Theological Works Tom. 3, Disp. 35 from thesis 14 to 20 inclusive, ending at last in these words of Bellarmine: We have no need here of Aristotle, since common sense suffices. For if it be allowed to affirm disparates properly of disparates, it will be allowed by the same right to affirm something of nothing, nothing of something, darkness of light, light of darkness, Belial of Christ, Christ of Belial: nor does our faith oblige us to defend what imply contradiction, p. 139.
pass_a.331: It does not help in this place to have objected personal predications, seeing that concerning them our former teacher B. Johannes Vorstius most rightly observes that in them not an abstract thing is predicated of an abstract, or — what is the same — a disparate abstract nature of a likewise disparate abstract nature, but a concrete of a concrete, whereas in our sacramental [proposition] an abstract is predicated of an abstract, body of bread, and so a disparate of a disparate.
pass_a.332: If you press with Johannes Musaeus’s peculiar disputation on the Sacred Supper opposed to Vorstius §. 99 — In the Sacramental proposition a Concrete is also in its way predicated of a Concrete, so that it is not said: the nature of this bread is the nature of Christ’s body, but only, this bread, namely Eucharistic, blessed bread, not common bread, but the Eucharist, consisting of two things, earthly and heavenly, is Christ’s body, citing Bajer Disp. on Impanation §.30 — besides that (1) he partly leaves the bread to be an abstract nature, inasmuch as merely Eucharistic or blessed and no longer common it by no means deserts its abstract nature or yields into a concrete: For bread (an abstract nature) does not by being blessed and separated by blessing from common use exchange abstract nature with concrete — otherwise every abstract thing separated by a peculiar blessing from common use would by that very fact be converted into a concrete; partly he confounds Eucharistic bread with the Eucharist, of which latter you may rightly say it consists of two things, earthly and heavenly, not likewise of the former except from a hypothesis assumed and not yet proved; also (2) it still remains that nonetheless the abstract nature of Christ’s body, or the abstract body of Christ, is predicated of the concrete, or of the composite of body and bread, and so this sacramental predication is unlike personal propositions (in which a concrete, not an abstract, is predicated of a Concrete). But when an abstract is predicated directly of a Concrete, as still a disparate of a disparate is predicated, so the predication cannot but be improper: for thus a part is predicated of a whole, and by this reason the predication is made synechdochic, consequently tropical or improper.
pass_a.333: (II) The GENERIC as nearer genus exhibits the sacramental proposition in which the thing signified is predicated of the sign. And although thus the predication can be proper when namely the Sign is materially the same as the thing signified, yet it cannot but be improper whenever sign and thing signified differ materially, whether the sign be held as merely signifying or further as exhibitive of the thing signified: For in either way the predication turns out metonymic or synechdochic, and so improper — in the former by metonymy of sign for thing signified; in the latter by metonymy of container for content, or by synecdoche of part for whole. It is confirmed that the horistic sacramental proposition is improper by its nature also by Induction of the several Sacramentals of both Old and New Testament occurring even in the Institution of the Sacred Supper itself.
pass_a.334: For when (a) in the Institution of Circumcision God addresses Abraham thus: This is my covenant between me and you and your seed after you, which you shall keep, that every male among you be circumcised, Gen. 17:10, God’s covenant is predicated of circumcision only improperly: For Circumcision is not properly the covenant but the sign of the covenant, God Himself interpreting in the next verse 11: You shall cut off the foreskin of the flesh, and this itself shall be the sign of the covenant between me and you. When (b) in the Institution of the Passover Moses in God’s name informs the whole people: The lamb to be eaten by you in the manner of those hastening is the Lord’s passover, Exod. 12:11; also: Take a lamb each householder for his family and slaughter the passover, v. 21; also: if anyone of you, while they eat the slaughtered lamb, asks what thing or office you are performing here? You shall answer: it is the Passover sacrifice of the Lord passing over the sons of Israel in Egypt, v. 27 — in all these propositions passover or passage is enunciated only improperly both of the lamb and of the slaughter and eating of the lamb, the substance of the lamb by no means to be converted into a transient action by any proper predication, and indeed by the same species of trope by which in the N.T. Christ Himself is called our passover, 1 Cor. 5:7, and also the rock that followed the Israelites in the desert: For a thing that signifies is wont to be named by the name of the thing it signifies, as it is written, the seven ears are seven years and many such. Hence it is that it was said the rock was Christ: for he did not say the rock signifies Christ, but as if this were so! Assuredly it was not this by substance but by signification — Augustine’s words, Questions on Leviticus 57.

329: §. III. The Reformed argue that the definitive Supper propositions — above all This is my body — are not proper but improper.
They reduce the proofs to two genera: the GENERIC and the SPECIFIC nature of the proposition taken materially.
330: As remoter genus, the GENERIC nature shows a disparate predicated of a disparate — whether τὸ hoc is bread alone, or bread with Christ’s body besides — once Carlstadt’s Identica This Body is my body is exploded as a novel fiction both Protestant sides hate.

Body predicated of bread is disparate of disparate; disparates force improper predication and shut out the proper — otherwise no improper speech would remain, and no metonymy or metaphor could exist except among disparates.

Gomarus builds this sharply (Tom. 3, Disp. 35, th. 14–20), ending with Bellarmine: common sense suffices — if disparates may be affirmed properly of disparates, one may as well affirm nothing of something, darkness of light, Belial of Christ (p. 139).
331: Objecting “personal” predications does not help here.
Vorstius notes that in those, a concrete is predicated of a concrete — not abstract disparate nature of abstract disparate nature.
In our sacramental saying, by contrast, abstract is predicated of abstract: body of bread, hence disparate of disparate.
332: Musaeus (§.99 vs Vorstius) claims the sacramental line somehow predicates concrete of concrete — this Eucharistic bread / Eucharist of two things is Christ’s body — citing Bajer on Impanation.
But blessing does not turn bread’s abstract nature into a concrete; and he conflates Eucharistic bread with the Eucharist itself.

Even then an abstract body is still predicated of a composite of body and bread — unlike personal propositions — so abstract of concrete remains disparate of disparate, a synecdoche, and thus improper.
333: (II) As nearer genus, the GENERIC view shows the sacramental proposition predicating the thing signified of the sign.

That can be proper only when sign and thing are materially the same; when they differ, the predication is metonymic or synechdochic — sign for thing, container for content, or part for whole — and so improper.
Induction from Old and New Testament sacramentals in the Supper’s own Institution confirms that a horistic sacramental proposition is improper by nature.
334: (a) In circumcision’s Institution (Gen. 17:10–11) God’s covenant is predicated of circumcision only improperly — circumcision is the sign of the covenant, God Himself explaining in the next verse.

(b) In the Passover Institution (Exod. 12:11, 21, 27) passover / passage is predicated only improperly of the lamb and of its slaughter and eating — the same species of trope by which Christ is our passover (1 Cor. 5:7) and the desert rock was Christ by signification, not substance (Augustine, Quaest. Lev. 57).
